label: paragraph_title
text:
APPEAL TO PRESIDENT
CALLES

label: text
text: TO END CONTROVERSY.

label: text
text:
Mexico City, August 19.
The Archbishop of Mexico, on behalf of the entire Catholic denomination, has memorallised President Calles asking for freedom of conscience, instruction, and Press, declaring that the Episcopate is yet at the same time patriotism and desire for peace and requesting President Calles to use his influence to persuade Congress to change the religious clauses of the Constitution and the penalties for disobedience of the new regulations.

label: text
text: Simultaneously a group of twenty Mexico City businessmen sent a letter to President Calles and the Episcopate proposing that they should confer to settle the controversy.

label: paragraph_title
text: ALLIED SUCCESSES.

label: text
text:
Peking, August 19.
The Allied troops claim successes on all fronts.

label: text
text: In conversation with Reuter's correspondent, a military officer, possessing the confidence of the Allied leaders, stated that the Allied plans at present were confined to the full of Kalgan. If the Kuomichun troops retreat to the North-West the "Allies would again discuss the situation.

label: text
text: It is asserted that Sun Chuan-Fang is working in fall agreement with Wu Pei-fu. The latter is concentrating his campaign in the North. When that has been brought to a successful conclusion, Wu Pei-fu will return to Hankow to superintend operations against the Southern "Reds."

label: text
text: This is not meant as subjugation of Tang Seng-chi but that Wu will institute a campaign designed to oust the "Reds" from Canton.

label: text
text: hang en-yuo, Yunnan's Fuchun, his assured the Allies of his support in the campaign against the "Rods."

label: text
text: The Cabinet, this morning resolved to elevate Chang Hsueh-liing to the rank of Marshall in recognition of his good work in the Nankow operations.—Reuter.

label: text
text: The Hunan troops, largely reinfreed by Cantonese yesterday commenced a general attack on the whole mile line. The attack is under the command of Tang Sengchi and Chiang Kai-shek, who are directing operations from Changsha, where they have established their headquarters. — Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: ARSENAL AND MINT

label: paragraph_title
text: REMOVED TO CHENCHOW BY GENERAL TANG.

label: text
text:
The frequent rumours that the Munition Factory and the "Mint in Changsha" would be removed to Chenzhou have turned out to be true, for General Tang Sherzschieh's troops recently began moving the machines and materials in the two factories to Chenzhou.
It is said that this move on five part of General Tang may be taken that he is making preparations in order to take up a position at Chenzhou in case of emergency, in view of the fact that Marshal Wu Fei-fu's troops, taking advantage

label: text
text: of the inactivity and impracticability of the movement of the Canton Revolutionary forces against the North and acting in concert with the navy in the Hsiankiang River are threatening to invade Hunan from Kiangsi Province. "Toho."

label: text

label: text
text: At five-thirty this morning Snigapore's first service of trolley buses came into operation, and thirty of those brightly-painted, capacious, and comfortable vehicles left the tramway depot according to their scheduled times to operate on the Geylang—Tanjong Pagar route.

label: text

label: text

label: text
text: The complete transformation of the present tram system will not be effected until 1928, when the Municipal programme of road reconstruction will be finished.

label: text
text: No alterations have been made in the schedule of fures now in operation.

label: paragraph_title
text:
EAST AND WEST.
MOVING ADDRESS TO
STUDENTS.

label: text
text: "His Excellency the Governor of Madras and party, after a tour in the Madura and Ramnad districts, have left, Kodaikural for Outace mund."

label: text
text: His Excellency addressing students of the High Clerc School, which is run on American lines for the education of American missionaries' children at Kodakamel-about their future, said as follows: "There will be the call of the lines of your adoption and there will be the call of your land in the West. But I would ask this of every one of you, that is to remember the

label: text
text: days when you were brought: up this country, whether you come back to it, or whether you spend your life in the West, for remember this, that this great land in which you are now can only make progression in the future and can only develop to its fullness, as we hope it will; if the West extends to it the hand of friendship and if the East and West advance together in the spirit of understanding of one another, in the spirit of sympathy with one another, and in the spirit of the desire to help one another. So I venture to hope that all of you who have been brought up in India will remember this and in "future life, whether you spend it here or in some other country, you will do your best to further and to encourage good relations between these two countries, out of gratitude for this country having been your early home, and because by so doing you will further the interests of these two great countries at the same time."

label: paragraph_title
text: OBITUARY.

label: paragraph_title
text: THE LATE CAPT. STACK.

label: text
text:
Singapore, August 14.
The late Captain Frederick James
Stack, whose death at the General
Hospital we reported yesterday,
came out to Singapore 27 years
ago. He joined the Straits Steam
ship Company in 1906, and when
he retired last year, owing to ill-
health, he was one of the senior
captain. Previous, to joining the
Straits Steamship Company he was
connected with the now defunct
Wee Bin and Co. and was in charge
of many of their China boats. The
funeral took place at Bidadari
Cemetery yesterday afternoon,
Archdencon Swindell offeinting.
Besides the relatives, those present
included:—Capt. J. Leighton, representing the Straits Merchant Service Guild, Capt. Weldon, the marine superintendent of the Straits Steamship Co., and Capt. J. Chalmers, senior boarding officer.

label: text

label: text
text: GOVERNMENT UNEASY.

label: text
text: The American Charge d'Affalres at Managuin reports that the Nicaragua Government is despatching troops in various directions to suppress the revolutionaries. Telephone and railway communications are interrupted.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: ANTI-TOBACCO.

label: text
text: MOVE TO PREVENT WOMEN SMOKING.

label: text
text: W. M. Mahoney, secretary of the anti-cigarette league, announced to-day that a convention of the organisation had been called for August 25, at Winona Lake, Indiana. At the meeting, a national campaign will be launched to seek legislation to prohibit women smoking and will attempt to prohibit all use of tobacco in any form. This is the first concerted anti-tobacco drive since the war, when the consumption of cigarettes increased fivefold owing to the demand from troops overseas and in training camps. The American consumption of cigarettes last year was about 75 billion. Fifteen years ago it was but seven billion.—“United Press.”

label: paragraph_title
text: MEXICAN MINERALS.

label: text
text:
COAL LANDS ARE NATIONAL.
PROPERTY.

label: text
text: "The government ruled to-day that coal deposits are national property as it recently declared petroleum is the property of the nation which is not a landholder."

label: text
text: The new mining laws which have just become effective by publication declare that all commercially valuable minerals and precious stones are the property of the nation. The laws will tremendously affect the mining industry of Mexico in which hundreds of millions of dollars of American money are invested.

label: text
text: Apparently existing concessions will be affirmed although "foreign "corporations under no circumstances can obtain mining concessions." Foreign individuals may obtain concessions only by waiving protection of their home governments insofar as Mexican investments are concerned. — Associated Press

label: paragraph_title
text: THE NEW TREATY.

label: text
text: LONDON PAPERS SAID TO RE ANGRY

label: text
text:
Rome, Aug. 14.
Local newspapers are giving unusual prominence to editorials from London newspapers denouncing the new Italo-Spanish treaty of friendship and co-operation signed three days ago by representatives of both governments.

label: text
text: The British viewpoint, as reflected in the Press, is that the treaty constitutes a serious menace against the peace of Europe in that it provides that Italy build warships for Spain. It is also a threat against the League of Nations, according to an excerpt taken from an editorial in the London "Daily Telegraph," "if it is true that the treaty contains a clause providing that in the event one signatory is attacked, the other will use its veto power in the council to prevent interference by the League.—United Press.

label: paragraph_title
text: PROHIBITION.

label: text
text:
POISONING CF ALCOHOL
STUDIED BY COOLIDGE.

label: text
text: Summer White House, Aug. 13.

label: text
text: President Coolidge made a careful examination of the order issued by the bureau of prohibition enforcement instructing manufacturers of industrial alcohol to increase the amount of poison which the law requires to be mixed with alcohol to make it unfit for beverage purposes.

label: text
text: The President took cognisance of the great volume of protests lodged against the order on the ground that it was illegal for the government to poison a food product because its use was contrary to law. The President sent a great mass of newspaper clippings and correspondence, without comment, to Assistant Secretary of the Treasury Winston.-United Press.

label: paragraph_title
text: BACON'S BILL.

label: text
text: NEW YORK "EVENING POST"

label: text
text: A NEW FRIEND

label: text
text: Colonel Thompson's attitude toward the Bacon Bill, giving the Moros a separate government under American protection, will decide the fate of that measure, in the opinion of the New York "Evening Post", which publishes a long editorial to-day favouring the bill. It expresses considerable doubts to the value of the Thompson mission but is willing to wait until it is known whether the Colonel will favour or oppose the Bacon Bill. If he favours it, says the editorial, the mission will have been worth while; if he opposes or ignores it, he will have missed an opportunity. The writer says that with Colonel Thompson's recommendation, President Coolidge could come out openly in favour of the bill, which would fail without presidential support.

label: text
text: It says that the purposes and results of the mission are still uncertain and it is well to await the complete report before indulging in criticism. However, it continues, it would have been better if President Coolidge had sent ex-Governor Cameron Forbes of Newton Gilbert, who are more familiar with the Philippines and the Filipinos than Colonel Thompson.

label: text
text: "Commenting directly on the Bacon Bill it asks, 'why shouldn't the United States take advantage of this opportunity to break the British and Dutch rubber monopoly?'". It says that the bill although ostensibly for the purpose of giving the Moros freedom has for its chief interest, the production of rubber "but there is room for both Moros and rubber."—"United Press."

label: paragraph_title
text: HUMBLE “SPUD.”

label: paragraph_title
text: MAY DISPLACE TASTY STRINGS IN ITALY.

label: text
text: Rome, August 11.

label: text
text: Perhaps Spaghetti and macaroni will face serious competition by the potato. If the plans of the Fascist Government work out successfully. Beginning to day restrictions were temporarily lifted on the importation of seed potatoes. The Government desires to increase the use of potato products in an attempt to induce the Italian people to forsake spaghetti and macaroni, which are made from wheat.

label: text
text: The Government has been anxious to cut down on wheat consumption as part of its economy campaign.—“China Press.

label: paragraph_title
text: MACE ABSENT.

label: text
text: IS THE BUSINESS PASSED

label: text
text: LEGAL?

label: text
text: CURIOUS SITUATION CREATED.

label: text
text: Poona, July 27.—A remarkable but apparently little-remarked incident occurred at "to-day's sitting of the Bombay Legislative Council whose Monsoon session commenced yesterday.

label: text
text:
The silver mace, which is usually placed on the Council Hall, is the table during the sittings, was not so placed, perhaps because the President was absent through in-disposition, the Vice-President taking the Chair instead. But after supplementary grants to the tune of nearly 20 lakhs had been passed, the mace was brought in.
The question was put whether business conducted without the mace was ultra vires or not, and does the mace indicate only the presence of the President or House in session, but no member, official or non-official, was able to throw light on the question when attention was drawn to the incident.

label: text
text: A free advertisement: crowds are seen daily at street corners in the concession, Kobe, watching the antics of small rubber ducks in a pail of water. The small ducks, which are sold at the phenomenal sum of 2 sen apiece, apparently move around in the water of their own volition and they dive and perform tail spins as well! Marvellous duck! The snag is that the water is dirty, but the casual observer does not observe that. And the ducks are tied to the tails of gold fish, whose frantic efforts to rid themselves of their floating burdens are responsible for the ducks' antics. This is a case for the attention of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals; the police also might not be remiss in taking a hand with this faldir.

label: text
text: Mr. Smith further stated that an extension of hours was necessary for the successful operation of the mining industry and that a national agreement for the settlement and regulation of wages was regarded by the workmen as essential in the best interests of the industry as a whole. Further, the Federation was prepared, after consideration of possible measures for the reorganisation of the industry to consider then what wages were possible. He also intimated that consideration of these things might possibly lead to an application to the Government for some assistance pending the completion of schemes for reorganisation. Mr. Williams, for the coal owners, made it perfectly clear that it would be useless to proceed whilst there was such a divergence of views upon what they considered to be cardinal points. On the question of hours he said that they considered the lengthening of the working day absolutely necessary to the continuance of the industry, and that it was their intention to implement the Eight Hours Act, recently passed and to take full advantage of its provisions. On wages, Mr. Williams said that the Mining Association could not consider what wages would be payable as districts composing that body in unmistakable language refused to allow anyone to determine the terms and conditions upon which work can be resumed in districts except by direct negotiations—with the representatives of their own men in the districts.

label: text
text: The Miners' statement concludes with a passage declaring the owners' attitude to be equivalent to a demand for direct surrender, and calling upon the miners to stiffen resistance and asking the public for support.—British Wireless Service.

label: text
text: The Trade Unions Congress has decided to appeal to the British Trade Unions and the International Federation of Trade Unions to organise a campaign for financial assistance from the Continental Unions. Trade Unions Congress representatives are going to Amsterdam for this purpose.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: No Government Intervention.

label: text
text: The Government does not intend to intervene in the coal dispute without a request by the parties.

label: text
text: Sir, A. Steel-Maitland has been delegated to act for the Government in any situation that may arise during the Recess. If the situation is unchanged, then developments are probable when the House of Commons re-assemblies on August 30 to confirm the Emergency Regulations.—Reuter.

label: text
text: London, later.

label: text
text: An important move is reported from Notts. The coalfield delegates, representing between 12,000 and 14,000 miners, have accepted the terms of the Bolsover Colliery Company of 7½ hours and the old wages arrangements. Signing on is commencing immediately.

label: text
text: The Derbyshire and others Notts owners have decided to open their pits on the same terms. —Reuter

label: paragraph_title
text: . Little Surprise.

label: text
text: Little surprise is expressed in the newspapers at the coal breakdown. Satisfaction, however, is felt that the conference was held as it has served to prove to the Government and the nation that the owners and miners stand exactly where they did a year ago, which some writers declare is precisely the intention of the miners' leaders, in order to throw the onus of action on to the Government.

label: text
text: The “Westminster Gazette” and “Dally News” boldly “assert than the responsibility nowlies with the Government.” The former is wondering whether it is not a duty for Mr. Baldwin to propose, or impose machinery, whereby the parties can be compelled to submit their claims to arbitration.

label: text
text:
The "Daily Herald" demands Government action.
The "Daily Express" and the "Daily Graphic" suggest that a way out could be found by the miners themselves returning to work in the districts, thus giving the leaders a choice between a settlement and a smashed Federation.—Reuter.
